'''''Scrophularia nodosa''''' (also called '''figwort''', '''woodland figwort''', and '''common figwort''') is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[herbaceous]] [[plant]] found in [[temperate region]]s of the [[Northern Hemisphere]] except western North America.<ref>Mills, S., The Complete Guide to Modern Herbalism, Thorsons, Great Britain, 1994.</ref> It grows in moist and cultivated waste ground.<ref>[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=SCNO2 PLANTS Profile for Scrophularia nodosa (woodland figwort) | USDA PLANTS<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

==Growth==
It grows upright, with thick, sharply square, [[succulent]] stems up to 150 cm tall from a horizontal [[rootstock]]. Its [[leaves]] are opposite, ovate at the base and lanceolate at the tip, all having toothed margins. The flowers are in loose [[inflorescence|cyme]]s in oblong or pyramidal [[panicle]]s. The individual flowers are globular, with five green [[sepal]]s encircling green or purple [[petals]], giving way to an egg-shaped [[seed]] capsule.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.purplesage.org.uk/profiles/figwort.htm |title=Figwort<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2007-05-03 |archive-date=2015-09-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923210932/http://www.purplesage.org.uk/profiles/figwort.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

[[Image:Warming-Skudbygning-Fig12-Scrophularia-nodosa.jpg|thumb|left|200px|First year Scrophularia nodosa plant: swollen [[hypocotyl]]/stem with scars from the first four pairs of leaves (1-4). From ([[Eugen Warming|Warming 1884]])]]

==Fossil record==
Seed identification of ''Scrophularia nodosa'' has been made from sub-stage IIIa of the [[Hoxnian]] at [[Clacton]] in [[Essex]], from the [[Middle Pleistocene]].<ref>The History of the British Flora, A  Factual Basis for Phytogeography by [[Sir Harry Godwin]], Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, {{ISBN|0 521 20254 X}}, 1975 edition page 318</ref>

==Folklore==
The plant was thought, by the [[doctrine of signatures]], to be able to cure the throat disease [[scrofula]] because of the throat-like shape of its flowers.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.questia.com/library/encyclopedia/figwort.jsp |title=Figwort |access-date=2017-09-11 |archive-date=2011-06-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605010625/http://www.questia.com/library/encyclopedia/figwort.jsp |url-status=dead }}</ref>
